top_authentic_signals.name: Live Web Fact-Checking (OSINT)
top_authentic_signals.summary: The research agent found credible reporting that corroborates the depicted event or scene.
top_authentic_signals.what_found: The video, known as "Gimbal," is authentic U.S. Navy footage recorded on January 21, 2015, by a fighter pilot from the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group. It first gained public attention in December 2017 through a New York Times article and was officially declassified and released by the Pentagon in April 2020. While the Pentagon states the object remains an "unidentified aerial phenomenon", skeptics like Mick West propose the object is likely an infrared glare from a distant jet, with the apparent rotation being an artifact of the camera's gimbal system.
top_authentic_signals.why_it_matters: Corroborated public reporting supports the underlying event or statement. It still does not prove the file is untouched, so the media-specific detectors remain important.
top_authentic_signals.caveat: OSINT is strongest for public figures, viral claims, and news events. Generic private video clips may have no searchable provenance.

top_ai_signals.name: Spectral Artifacts
top_ai_signals.summary: The Six-Lens model scored this image 79.3% AI and 20.7% authentic, a extremely high-confidence finding toward synthetic generation.
top_ai_signals.what_found: All six spectral lenses, covering visual texture (ConvNeXt), frequency grids (FFT), sensor noise simulation (SRM), color-space fingerprints (YCbCr), spatial reconstruction (SPAI), and robustness testing, collectively scored this image 79.3% AI. At this level, the majority of lenses independently flagged patterns like periodic frequency grids and noise distributions inconsistent with any known camera sensor profile.
top_ai_signals.why_it_matters: This model looks for patterns invisible to the human eye, buried in the pixel-level math of the image. A 79.3% score means the statistical fingerprint aligns significantly more with AI generation than camera physics, and these frequency-domain traces are very hard to remove without visibly degrading the image.
top_ai_signals.caveat: Heavy JPEG compression, aggressive resizing, or strong image filters can partially destroy the frequency-domain signals this model depends on, potentially softening a confident AI detection into an inconclusive result. Conversely, very new or unusual AI generators not present in training data may produce lower-than-expected scores.
